title: Cannabis Root, Foliar & Flower Disease Differentials

content.overview: Cannabis can be affected by root/crown pathogens, powdery mildew, Botrytis and other disease problems, but similar crop symptoms can also arise from environmental, irrigation or root-zone stress. Specialist diagnosis integrates crop stage, tissue affected, signs, environment and testing.

vocabulary.definition: Disease affecting roots or basal stem/crown tissues, often requiring separation from waterlogging, oxygen stress and other root-zone disorders.
A fungal disease characterized by superficial powdery colonies on susceptible plant surfaces; confirmation should use organism evidence rather than leaf discoloration alone.
A fungal pathogen associated with gray mold/bud rot under favorable host and environmental conditions.

sections.title: Root and crown cases need root-zone context
sections.body: Root browning, poor uptake, wilt and reduced vigor may reflect pathogens such as Fusarium or Pythium-like organisms, but waterlogging, low oxygen and root-zone management can produce overlapping findings. Inspect roots and reconstruct irrigation/environment history.

sections.title: Visible fungal growth can strengthen, not replace, the workup
sections.body: Powdery colonies or gray sporulation can provide useful direct evidence, while environmental conditions and crop density help explain risk. Preserve sample identity and escalate uncertain or high-consequence cases.

sections.title: Management begins with source reduction and environment
sections.body: Integrated disease management emphasizes clean stock, sanitation, water/environment management, monitoring and appropriate biological/biorational or other authorized controls. Treatment legality and product selection remain jurisdiction- and label-specific.

workedExamples: A flowering canopy with localized gray mold after prolonged humidity excursions supports a Botrytis workup, but affected tissue should still be documented and handled under the facility's contamination/disposition procedure.
commonMistakes: Assuming all root browning is infectious.
Calling nutrient or light stress a disease without pathogen evidence.
Turning a literature control category into unauthorized pesticide or sanitizer use.
content.practicalApplication: Build a three-column differential for one root/crown, one foliar and one flower disease scenario: supporting evidence, conflicting evidence and next confirmation step.
content.summary: Cannabis disease differentials combine organism evidence with environmental/root-zone context and do not collapse overlapping symptoms into premature certainty.
